forces.title: Macro tailwinds for PE buyout funds have diminished
forces.description: Between 2010-2017, PE buyout funds benefited from strong macro tailwinds like cheap financing and expanding deal multiples, allowing elevated entry prices to be overcome. However, in the 2018-2023 period, these tailwinds have significantly diminished, making purchase price discipline a far more critical factor for generating strong returns. This shift necessitates greater strategic rigor in dealmaking.
forces.source_title: Private equity confirms a timeless principle: Purchase price matters

forces.title: Record high entry multiples shrink PE margin for error
forces.description: Globally, buyout entry multiples reached a record average of 11.8 times EBITDA in 2025, climbing to 18.1 times for transactions over $500 million. These elevated premiums, often justified by "A-grade" businesses, significantly shrink the margin for error for PE sponsors, especially with less leverage doing the work. This intensifies the pressure on GPs to demonstrate operational improvements for value creation.
forces.source_title: Private equity confirms a timeless principle: Purchase price matters

forces.title: Deployment pressure and asset competition drive PE premiums
forces.description: General Partners (GPs) face intense pressure to deploy capital, along with fierce competition for high-quality assets. These factors, alongside underwriting AI and GP confidence levels, contribute to higher purchase price multiples. This environment compels GPs to justify premiums for "durable, A-grade businesses," but paying such high multiples significantly reduces the margin for error and increases the importance of post-acquisition value creation.
forces.source_title: Private equity confirms a timeless principle: Purchase price matters

forces.title: Digital infrastructure universe expands, diversifying PE/VC asset classes
forces.description: The digital infrastructure sector has expanded dramatically beyond traditional communications assets, now encompassing edge facilities, power-linked assets, chip producers, and AI-adjacent businesses. This expansion significantly enlarges the opportunity set for investors, including PE/VC funds, but also increases control challenges. Value creation now depends on a wider range of asset-level portfolio choices, demanding a deeper understanding of where value will accrue.
forces.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

forces.title: AI infrastructure expands digital asset class for PE/VC
forces.description: The expanding boundary of digital infrastructure now explicitly includes AI infrastructure, such as computing-power-intensive data halls, power interconnection assets, and cooling systems. This structural shift diversifies portfolios for PE/VC investors but also increases sensitivity to utilization, customer mix, and supply chain constraints. It demands adapted underwriting and strategic frameworks to capture value in this swiftly expanding and complex asset class.
forces.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

forces.title: Misclassification of digital infrastructure assets creates valuation gaps
forces.description: Assets previously grouped under a common infrastructure label are now exhibiting diverging economic behaviors, leading to visible costs of misclassification for investors. Execution-heavy and transitional assets (e.g., B2C fiber, cable) face wider valuation gaps and longer exit timelines compared to well-understood core data centers. PE/VC firms risk holding, valuing, and selling assets under assumptions that no longer match actual performance, demanding deeper due diligence.
forces.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

forces.title: Infrastructure asset holding periods extend due to market shifts
forces.description: The average infrastructure asset holding period stretched to 7.6 years in 2025, up from 6.1 years in 2021, according to BCG analysis of top 50 infrastructure general partners. This increase reflects challenges such as wider valuation gaps, longer exit timelines, and investor reassessments of operational complexity in execution-heavy assets. Extended hold periods can tie up capital and delay distributions for PE/VC funds.
forces.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

forces.title: High valuations impede European digital infrastructure deals
forces.description: In Europe, 78% of surveyed investors cited valuation gaps as the primary barrier to digital infrastructure deal completion in 2025, a significant increase from 48% year-on-year. Similarly, 63% of US respondents cited high valuations as a top obstacle. This environment makes dealmaking more challenging for PE/VC, necessitating greater precision in underwriting and potentially longer negotiation periods to bridge buyer-seller expectations.
forces.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

forces.title: Revenue growth drives infrastructure enterprise value, not multiples
forces.description: From 2020 to 2025, 79% of enterprise value growth in global infrastructure deals came from revenue growth, surpassing margin or multiple expansion. This indicates a fundamental shift for PE/VC investors, who must now focus on improving the operating performance of underlying businesses rather than relying on rerating valuations. This demands a more hands-on, operational value creation strategy to generate strong returns.
forces.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

forces.title: Asset-heavy Telco NetCo spinouts show negative shareholder returns
forces.description: BCG's 2026 Telco Value Creators Report indicates that asset-heavy NetCos, spun out from operating telco businesses, delivered a five-year total shareholder return of -4%. This represents the weakest performance among all telco archetypes, highlighting a significant risk for PE/VC firms considering or invested in similar structural separations within the telecommunications sector. It underscores the need for careful portfolio decomposition and asset-specific capital strategies.
forces.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

forces.title: Operators recompose portfolios, repurpose assets for AI-driven growth
forces.description: Operators are shifting from broad structural separations to asset-specific allocation, decomposing portfolios to match each asset/service to the optimal ownership model, capital strategy, and value creation path. This includes repurposing existing real estate, central offices, and fiber infrastructure for data centers and high-capacity networks to capture AI-driven upside. This strategy allows PE/VC to unlock greater value through partnerships, joint ventures, and targeted investments.
forces.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

forces.title: Opportunistic M&A in Irish hospitality driven by operator pressures
forces.description: M&A activity in the Irish hospitality sector is expected to remain opportunistic, with well-capitalised groups positioned to acquire or reinvest. Pressures like cost inflation, succession issues, and capital expenditure requirements create opportunities for PE/VC firms to acquire smaller operators. This environment supports value creation through operational improvements, repositioning, energy efficiency, or brand-led strategies for acquired assets.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Hospitality Sector H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook July 2026

forces.title: Companies reshape portfolios, pursue focused tuck-in M&A
forces.description: Companies are advised to actively reshape their portfolios by divesting noncore businesses and pursuing focused tuck-in M&A, while avoiding transformative deals that strain the balance sheet. This investor strategy implies that PE/VC firms, in their role as owners, must drive portfolio optimization and disciplined M&A to enhance value. The focus is on strategic adjustments to existing businesses rather than large, risky acquisitions.
forces.source_title: Investors Believe in AI—Now They Want Results

forces.title: Growth and return on capital become key investment considerations
forces.description: Investors prioritize long-term organic growth outlook and return on capital as the most important metrics for investment decisions, shifting emphasis from short-term momentum. For PE/VC firms, this means value creation strategies must robustly demonstrate sustainable growth and efficient capital deployment within portfolio companies. This elevates the importance of operational improvements and strategic reinvestment over financial engineering.
forces.source_title: Investors Believe in AI—Now They Want Results

forces.title: Investors demand lower leverage, accountable AI capex from companies
forces.description: Investors are signaling a preference for companies to avoid high leverage (staying below 3x net debt to EBITDA) and to treat AI capital expenditure as an investment with accountable payback, without significantly diluting margins or excessive leveraging. This influences PE/VC financial strategies, demanding more conservative capital structures and rigorous ROI analysis for AI investments within portfolio companies.
forces.source_title: Investors Believe in AI—Now They Want Results

forces.title: Operating performance drives PE value amid reduced leverage
forces.description: With less buyout value coming from leverage and multiple expansion (down from nearly 60% between 2010-2022 to record multiples by 2025), operating performance must now "carry more of the load" for private equity value creation. This structural shift means PE firms need to focus intensively on improving the fundamental business operations of their portfolio companies rather than relying primarily on financial engineering or market tailwinds for returns.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: Lengthening PE hold periods, slower exit rates challenge funds
forces.description: Average hold periods for private equity investments have extended to over six and a half years. Only 19% of 2021 acquisitions were sold by 2025, significantly below the typical 30% four-year exit rate of the prior decade. This trend ties up capital for longer, impacting fund liquidity and potentially Distributed-to-Paid-in (DPI) ratios. This forces PE firms to adapt their value creation strategies for extended ownership cycles.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: Buyout distributions decline significantly relative to AUM
forces.description: Buyout distributions fell to 6% of assets under management (AUM) in 2025, a notable drop from an average of 16% between 2015 and 2019. This significant decline reflects the challenges of slower exits and extended hold periods, directly impacting Limited Partners' (LPs) ability to receive capital back from funds. This pressure intensifies the need for PE firms to find new ways to accelerate realizations and improve DPI.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: Geopolitical fragmentation and Gen AI reshape PE portfolio companies
forces.description: Geopolitical fragmentation is altering supply chains and routes to market, while Generative AI is reshaping cost structures and growth models within portfolio companies. These underlying business changes are accelerating, requiring private equity firms to adopt more dynamic and flexible value creation strategies. This dual pressure demands a keen focus on resilience, technological adoption, and strategic adaptation to maintain competitiveness and drive returns.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: PE firms double operating groups, expand specialized capabilities
forces.description: Since 2021, private equity firms have more than doubled the size of their operating groups on average, simultaneously expanding specialized capabilities and engaging operating teams earlier in the investment life cycle. This indicates a structural shift towards more hands-on, operational value creation, moving beyond reliance on financial engineering. This investment aims to streamline execution and capture value more quickly from portfolio companies.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: Enterprise transformation now standard for PE portfolio companies
forces.description: Over 80% of PE executives report at least one portfolio company undergoing transformation, with 70% noting an increase in this proportion over the last three to five years. This indicates that enterprise transformation has become the new normal for PE-backed businesses. Firms are now adopting integrated value creation agendas, examining operations, commercial performance, pricing, technology, and organizational effectiveness together to uncover larger, systemic opportunities.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: Periodic re-underwriting of portfolio companies
forces.description: Leading PE firms are adopting periodic "re-underwriting" or "rediligence" as a mechanism to reset portfolio companies' ambition every two or three years. This process involves deal teams and operating partners examining changes in markets, competition, operational performance, and future value sources, going beyond initial investment theses. This systematic approach allows firms to identify and capture additional value beyond initial acquisition assumptions.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: European PE fund uses dedicated exit-readiness for faster exits
forces.description: A European private equity fund created a dedicated portfolio and exit-readiness function, using senior partners to challenge assumptions and assess an asset's appeal to a future buyer. This rigorous, recurring management discipline has accelerated its exits by about 40% and substantially increased distributions to investors (around €2 billion distributed, equivalent to one-third of AUM). This proactive approach surfaces risks earlier and strengthens the equity story for sale.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: Investing in full-time transformation leadership for portfolio companies
forces.description: Over 60% of private equity firms are now deploying full-time Chief Transformation Officers (CTOs) within portfolio companies to support more intensive execution demands. These CTOs are accountable for the entire value creation program, coordinating across functions and driving urgency. This approach expands executive bandwidth and, in one case, increased execution speed by a factor of five, leading to faster value capture and higher-performing programs.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: AI accelerates portfolio re-underwriting, enabling faster value assessment
forces.description: AI is significantly reducing the time required for PE firms to reassess value during the hold period, transforming re-underwriting from weeks to days by leveraging large data sets from prior transformations. This enables deal teams to test assumptions more frequently and in greater depth, leading to quicker identification of value creation opportunities and potential risks within portfolio companies. This enhanced agility improves investment management.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: AI integration drives cost reduction and new product development in PE portfolios
forces.description: AI is directly contributing to performance within PE portfolio companies, notably reducing content production costs by 40% and customer care costs by 15% through automation and improved routing. Additionally, AI enables the launch of new products and enhances commercial performance through data-driven models. This integration of AI into corporate budgets moves it beyond a "science project," driving tangible operational efficiencies and new revenue streams.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: Centralized AI capabilities support PE portfolio companies
forces.description: Some PE firms are coordinating AI efforts centrally by establishing shared AI teams or Centers of Excellence. These provide common tools, vendor access, technical expertise, and support for evaluating use cases across portfolio companies. One global fund created an AI COE to assess ROI, vet vendors, and maintain a common playbook. This approach ensures efficient AI deployment, scales successful applications, and shortens feedback loops between operational performance and investment decisions.
forces.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

forces.title: High investor demand fuels AI-enabled business models and VC funding
forces.description: AI start-ups received half of all global venture capital funding in 2025, driven by strong investor demand for AI-enabled business models. This creates a significant tailwind for the PE/VC sector, not only in backing AI-native companies but also in accelerating AI adoption and scaling across existing portfolio companies to enhance their competitive positioning and value.
forces.source_title: Beyond productivity: How AI creates value in private equity

forces.title: Digital and AI leadership drives superior TSR for PE-backed companies
forces.description: PE-backed companies leading in digital and AI initiatives delivered significantly higher Total Shareholder Return (TSR) CAGR than laggards between 2018 and 2022 (e.g., 6.1x higher in insurance, 2.9x in consumer, 2.3x in energy/materials). This highlights a substantial value creation opportunity for PE firms in accelerating AI adoption and scaling across their portfolio companies, beyond just investing in AI-native businesses, to enhance competitive positioning.
forces.source_title: Beyond productivity: How AI creates value in private equity

forces.title: AI-augmented workflows boost revenue per employee, operational efficiency
forces.description: AI is increasingly used to streamline sales processes, automate customer service, generate marketing content, and automate client onboarding, enhancing commercial performance and making operating models more scalable. This leads to significant gains, such as a $180,000 increase in median revenue per employee (52% jump from Level 3 AI maturity). For PE/VC, this means higher bottom lines and overcoming talent constraints, driving material value creation in portfolio companies.
forces.source_title: Beyond productivity: How AI creates value in private equity

viewpoints.title: Purchase price discipline increasingly critical for private equity buyout fund returns
viewpoints.description: McKinsey states that purchase price discipline has become more critical for PE buyout funds in the 2018-2023 vintage cluster, contrasting with the 2010-2017 boom. During the boom, cheap financing and expanding multiples masked high entry prices. However, in recent years, disciplined buyers (lowest-price quartile) delivered 3.4x MOIC, significantly outperforming those who paid highest PPMs (2.7x). This indicates that macro tailwinds have diminished, making careful acquisition pricing a more pronounced determinant of success for PE funds.
viewpoints.source_title: Private equity confirms a timeless principle: Purchase price matters

viewpoints.title: Investors too optimistic on AI development and regulation in market pricing
viewpoints.description: According to BCG's 2026 Global Investor Survey, there's significant net optimism (45%) that the market is too optimistic regarding how AI development and regulation are reflected in current market pricing. This suggests that while investors believe in AI's potential, they perceive valuations as potentially inflated, raising concerns about future returns. This sentiment implies a need for PE/VC to conduct rigorous due diligence on AI-related investments to avoid overpaying.
viewpoints.source_title: Investors Believe in AI—Now They Want Results

viewpoints.title: Valuation multiple compression shifts total shareholder return to fundamental improvements
viewpoints.description: BCG's 2026 Global Investor Survey indicates that 73% of investors believe potential compression of valuation multiples will make companies' Total Shareholder Return (TSR) increasingly dependent on improved fundamentals like growth, margin expansion, and free cash flow generation. This implies a more challenging environment for PE/VC firms that previously relied on multiple expansion for returns. Value creation strategies must now emphasize operational excellence and fundamental business improvements to deliver investor returns.
viewpoints.source_title: Investors Believe in AI—Now They Want Results

viewpoints.title: Private equity shifting to adaptive, execution-led value creation models
viewpoints.description: McKinsey states that private equity firms are increasingly shifting towards adaptive, execution-led models to reshape value creation during their ownership periods. This is driven by the shrinking half-life of initial deal theses and the necessity for operating performance to carry more of the load, as leverage and multiple expansion contribute less to buyout value. Leading firms are now focusing on re-underwriting value, embracing enterprise transformation, investing in dedicated transformation leadership, mobilizing employees, and integrating AI.
viewpoints.source_title: Unlocking full potential: Five practices reshaping PE value creation

viewpoints.title: Broad AI adoption yields significantly higher revenue multiples for PE-backed companies
viewpoints.description: McKinsey states that PE-backed companies broadly embracing AI achieve median revenue multiples more than twice those focusing solely on productivity initiatives. Their analysis of 471 PE-backed companies shows Level Four AI adopters trade at a median revenue multiple of 31x, compared to 13x for Level One. This indicates that integrating AI across operations, products, and new business ventures, beyond mere productivity, is a powerful, yet underutilized, catalyst for substantial value creation and higher valuations in the private equity sector.
viewpoints.source_title: Beyond productivity: How AI creates value in private equity

Key adjacency as AI acts in the physical world; common operating layers (edge inference, sensors, robot operating systems, fleet management) across use cases like warehouse automation and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) could deliver platform economics and utilization characteristics attractive to infrastructure investors.

Next-generation, high-capacity, physically diverse fiber infrastructure connecting AI and hyperscale data centers in new power/land-available markets; addresses mismatch between computing power location and network capacity; opportunity in funding/aggregating scarce rights-of-way and access infrastructure via anchor-backed platforms.
